Andrea Palladio. The Venetian architect whose rational interpretation of classical Roman design established principles of proportion and symmetry that dominated architecture for centuries.

Palladio lived from 1508 to 1580. His most iconic work is the Villa Rotonda, completed around 1567 near Vicenza. It's a symmetrical villa with a domed rotunda and classical portico on all four sides, embodying ideal proportions and harmony. He created the Basilica of Vicenza between 1546 and 1617, a civic building that wrapped a medieval structure in classical colonnades and reconciled antiquity with medieval forms.

Palladio designed numerous Venetian villas for wealthy merchants, establishing the Palladian villa typology: symmetrical, classically porticoed, and integrated into agricultural estates. He studied Roman ruins and the treatises of Vitruvius, extracting principles of proportion and order that he applied to contemporary buildings. He pioneered the use of the classical portico as the dominant facade element, a feature adopted globally and becoming central to neoclassical architecture.

Perhaps his most influential contribution was publishing I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura, the Four Books of Architecture, in 1570. This systematized classical orders and proportional systems and became the most influential architectural treatise of the Renaissance. His work influenced Thomas Jefferson, Christopher Wren, and nearly every eighteenth-century architect, becoming the foundation of Palladianism—an international architectural movement that influenced neoclassical design through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

Palladio was the defining architect of the mature Renaissance, and his rational classicism advanced the movement's ideals. He revived and systematized classical principles, and his treatises codified the classical architectural language for centuries to come. He established the palatial country villa as a major architectural type that would endure.
